html:
The resettlement of the people of Banaba, a small phosphate island in the central Pacific, to Rabi Island in Fiji at the end of 1945, after mining and war had made their home almost unlivable.

Banaba, also called Ocean Island, lay in the British colony of the Gilbert and Ellice Islands, now Kiribati. Phosphate was found there in 1900, as on Nauru, and mining by British companies stripped most of the island over the following decades. The Banabans were paid little. In 1942 the colony bought Rabi, in Fiji, with money from phosphate royalties, as a future home. That year Japan occupied Banaba, deported most of the people to other islands, and killed many of those who remained.

After the war the British gathered about a thousand Banabans and Gilbertese and took them to Rabi, saying Banaba could not support them. In the 1970s Banaban leaders sued the British government in London over their treatment, winning a moral victory but little money. The Banabans of Rabi became Fijian citizens, with their own council, while keeping ties to Banaba.
sum: The resettlement of the people of Banaba, a small phosphate island in the central Pacific, to Rabi Island in Fiji at the end of 1945, after mining and war had made their home almost unlivable.
